name: simple sugars Sucrose
notes: Presence of sucrose metabolism genes indicates microbial potential to degrade, transform, or utilize sucrose.

name: simple sugars Mannose
notes: Presence of mannose metabolism genes indicates microbial potential to utilize mannose-containing carbohydrates, supporting turnover of plant- and microbial-derived sugar compounds.

name: simple sugars Galactose
notes: Presence of galactose metabolism genes indicates microbial potential to utilize galactose derived from plant polysaccharides, glycoproteins, or other organic matter inputs.

name: simple sugars Fucose
notes: Presence of fucose metabolism genes indicates microbial potential to utilize fucose-containing glycans derived from host mucins, dietary fiber, or microbial cell surfaces. Fucose liberation is a key step in mucin glycan catabolism and supports cross-feeding among specialist gut microbes including Bacteroides and Bifidobacterium species.

name: simple sugars Xylose
notes: Presence of xylose metabolism genes indicates microbial potential to utilize xylose, a major hemicellulose-derived sugar, linking plant polymer breakdown to downstream carbon metabolism.

name: simple sugars Fructose
notes: Presence of fructose metabolism genes indicates microbial potential to utilize fructose and fructose-containing oligosaccharides (FOS, inulin) derived from dietary sources such as fruits, vegetables, and prebiotic supplements. Fructose fermentation supports microbial growth and short-chain fatty acid production in the colon.

name: simple sugars Arabinose
notes: Presence of arabinose metabolism genes indicates microbial potential to utilize arabinose, a common component of hemicellulose and pectin-derived plant carbohydrates.

name: simple sugars Rhamnose
notes: Presence of rhamnose metabolism genes indicates microbial potential to utilize rhamnose-containing plant or microbial polysaccharides, supporting turnover of complex sugar inputs.

name: Cellulose
notes: A genome is capable of cellulose degradation if it encodes at least one endo-acting cellulase, one exo-acting cellobiohydrolase, and one β-glucosidase. LPMOs [AA9, AA10, AA16] provide an oxidative bonus that enhances but is not essential for cellulose degradation.

name: Hemicellulose
notes: For a genome to have hemicellulose degradation capability, it should encode: at least one backbone hydrolase, one side-chain/esterase, and optionally an LPMO for enhanced activity.

name: Pectin
notes: For a genome to have pectin degradation capability, it should encode: at least one backbone-cleaving hydrolase or lyase, one debranching or accessory enzyme, and one esterase for de-methylation or de-acetylation.

name: Core Mucin Glycan Degradation
notes: Core mucin glycan degradation requiring the minimum enzymatic toolkit to access mucin sugars. GH33 sialidases remove terminal sialic acid residues, GH29/GH95 fucosidases remove fucose, and GH20/GH35 target the core N-acetylglucosamine and galactose residues beneath. Represents the "core GH-ome" for mucin degradation identified across specialist gut microbes including Akkermansia muciniphila and Bacteroides spp

name: Extended Mucin Glycan Degradation
notes: Extended mucin glycan degradation capturing capacity to degrade internal glycan structures beyond the terminal sugar layer. Requires sialidase and fucosidase for outer layer removal, plus at least one enzyme from each inner glycan group: GlcNAc/GalNAc-acting enzymes, N-acetylgalactosaminidases, and galactosidases. GH16 endo-acting O-glycanases are included in gene_ids as indicators of enhanced degradation capacity but not required by the rule. Genomes satisfying this rule likely represent specialist mucin degraders with capacity to access and ferment deeply buried glycan structures.
gene_ids: GH33, GH29, GH95, GH84, GH85, GH89, GH20, GH101, GH129, GH2, GH35, GH42, GH98, GH16

name: RS granule degradation
notes: Core resistant starch degradation capacity requiring a GH13 α-amylase with granule-binding CBM domain. CBM20 and CBM26 facilitate physical attachment to semi-crystalline RS granule surfaces, enabling endo-acting hydrolysis of α-1,4 linkages. Characteristic of primary RS degraders including Ruminococcus bromii and RS-degrading Bifidobacterium adolescentis strains. Genomes satisfying this rule without extended capacity likely represent partial RS degraders dependent on cross-feeding from specialist primary degraders.

name: α‑glucan processing
notes: Extended resistant starch degradation requiring GH13 α-amylase with granule-binding CBM (CBM20 or CBM26) plus accessory α-glucan processing: GH31 (α-glucosidase, removes α-1,6 branch points) or GH77 (4-α-glucanotransferase, chain rearrangement). Genomes satisfying this rule have fuller α-glucan processing capacity beyond initial granule attack, characteristic of thorough RS degraders such as Ruminococcus bromii and some Bifidobacterium strains.
gene_ids: GH13, GH57, GH77, GH31, CBM20, CBM26

name: Acetate-Final
notes: Union of all genes across Acetate-1, Acetate-2, and Acetate-3 pathways. Summary rule pointing to three acetate production routes.
Acetate via pyruvate decarboxylation (PDH/PFOR/PFL) → acetyl-CoA → phosphotransacetylase/acetate kinase or ADP-forming acetyl-CoA synthetase route.
Acetate via aldehyde oxidation: pyruvate → acetaldehyde → acetate via aldehyde dehydrogenase, combined with acetyl-CoA intermediate step.
Acetate via direct hydrolysis: acetyl-CoA hydrolase (K01895) or acetate/butyrate-CoA ligase (K01913).
Pyruvate decarboxylation sub-module used across multiple acetate routes; covers PDH (K00163/K00161/K00162) and PFL (K01568).

name: Propionate-Final
notes: Union of all genes across Propionate-1 (methylmalonyl-CoA), Propionate-2 (acrylate/lactate), and Propionate-3 (propionyl-CoA) routes.

Propionate via methylmalonyl-CoA pathway: succinyl-CoA intermediates (K01899/K01900/K01902/K01903), methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (K01847/K01849/K01848), and propionyl-CoA carboxylase (K00140) or epimerase (K05606). Dominant route in Bacteroidota and Prevotella.
Propionate via acrylate pathway: propionate-CoA transferase (K01026), lactoyl-CoA dehydratase (K20626/K20627), propionyl-CoA reductase (K00248/K00232). Characteristic of Megasphaera, Coprococcus.
Propionate via propionyl-CoA pathway: propanediol dehydratase (K01699/K13919/K13920), propionaldehyde dehydrogenase (K13922). Found in Roseburia inulinivorans and related organisms.

Shared acetate/propionate intermediate sub-rule: phosphotransacetylase/acetate kinase route or aldehyde/ferredoxin oxidoreductase combined with kinase. Used as alternative completion route in Propionate-1/2/3.
Propionyl-CoA → propionate completion step: AMP-forming propionate-CoA ligase (K01895) or propionyl-CoA synthetase (K01908).

name: Butyrate-Final
notes: Union of all genes across Butyrate-1 (acetyl-CoA condensation), Butyrate-2 (glutarate), Butyrate-3 (lysine), and Butyrate-4 (4-aminobutyrate) routes.

Butyrate via classical acetyl-CoA condensation: thiolase (K00626), hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase, crotonase/enoyl-CoA hydratase, butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase (Butyrate-sub1), phosphotransbutyrylase/butyrate kinase (Butyrate-sub1 thiokinase).

Butyrate via glutarate/lysine 5-aminopentanoate pathway: glutaconate CoA-transferase (K00135/K08324/K00139/K17761) plus lysine-2,3-aminomutase module (Butyrate-sub2) and terminal thiokinase (Butyrate-sub1).
Butyrate via lysine pathway: L-lysine 2,3-aminomutase (K01580), butyrate biosynthesis from β-lysine (K13524/K07250/K14268/K00823/K16871), plus Butyrate-sub2 and Butyrate-sub1.
Butyrate via 4-aminobutyrate (GABA) pathway: 4-aminobutyrate CoA-transferase (K01843), combined with Butyrate-1 pathway completion. Rare pathway found in Clostridiales.
Terminal butyrate release sub-module: butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase electron transfer (K00209/K17829) and phosphotransbutyrylase/butyrate kinase (K01034/K01035) or butyrate-CoA ligase (K19709).

Glutarate to glutaryl-CoA sub-module for Butyrate-2 and Butyrate-3: glutarate CoA-transferase isoforms (K00043/K08318/K18120/K18121), glutaconyl-CoA decarboxylase beta subunit (K18122), and glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase (K14534).

name: Formate
notes: Pyruvate formate lyase (K00656) catalyzes pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + formate under anaerobic conditions. Formate is a major fermentation product in mixed-acid fermenters (E. coli, Prevotella spp.) and feeds cross-feeding networks with methanogens and acetogens.

name: Lactate-Final
notes: Union of all genes across Lactate-1, Lactate-2, and Lactate-3 routes. Summarizes L-lactate and D-lactate production capacity.

L-lactate via homolactic or heterolactic fermentation: glycolytic intermediate supply (Lactate-sub1), glycolytic redox (K00134/K00150, K00927, K01837) or phosphogluconate route (K11389/K00131/K18978), and L/D-lactate dehydrogenase (K01689/K27394/K00873/K12406) combined with LDH (K00016).
L-lactate dehydrogenase (K00016) alone. Permissive rule detecting LDH presence as a proxy for lactate production or consumption capacity.

D-lactate via methylglyoxal pathway: methylglyoxal synthase (K18124/K18125), lactoylglutathione lyase (K01053), hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase (K05308), and glyoxalase (K11395/K18127), combined with LDH (K00016).

Upper glycolysis/pentose phosphate supply module shared across Lactate-1 and other fermentation rules. Encodes hexokinase, phosphoglucose isomerase, fructose bisphosphate aldolase, and triose phosphate isomerase for pyruvate supply.

name: Ethanol
notes: Ethanol production via two routes: (1) pyruvate → acetaldehyde → ethanol via bifunctional alcohol/aldehyde dehydrogenase (K01568) plus ADH (K00001/K00121/K13953); (2) acetaldehyde oxidation via aldehyde dehydrogenase (K04072) plus ALDH (K00128/K00149) and acetyl-CoA route (K01895).

name: Methanol
notes: Pectinesterase (pme); releases methanol as byproduct of dietary pectin demethylation. Primary source of gut methanol

name: Succinate production
notes: A genome is considered capable of succinate production via the reductive branch of the TCA pathway if it encodes: an anaplerotic carboxylation enzyme (PEP carboxykinase K01610 or pyruvate carboxylase K01958/K01959), malate dehydrogenase (K00024), fumarase (K01676–K01678), and fumarate reductase (K00244–K00247). This captures the PEP/pyruvate → oxaloacetate → malate → fumarate → succinate route described for gut anaerobes (e.g., Bacteroides/Prevotella) that produce succinate as a major fermentation end product in the colon.

name: Succinate consumption
notes: Co-occurrence of succinyl-CoA synthetase (K01899, K01900), methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (K01847, K01848), and methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase (K05606) defines the core succinate → succinyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA branch of the succinate-to-propionate pathway.

name: Oxygen - Low Affinity Use
notes: Low affinity oxygen use indicates an aerobe and requires the presence of a low-affinity oxidase plus a majority of the elctron transport chain

name: Oxygen - High Affinity Use
notes: High affinity oxygen use indicates a microaerophile and requires the presence of a high-affinity oxidase plus a majority of the elctron transport chain

name: Dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium DNRA
notes: DNRA reduces nitrate to ammonium through a two-step process: nitrate reduction via Nar or Nap systems, followed by nitrite reduction via Nrf or Nir enzymes. Presence of one nitrate reductase system and one nitrite reductase system indicates DNRA capability.

name: Nitrate reduction to Nitrite
notes: Nitrate reduction to nitrite can occur through either the membrane-bound Nar system (K00370, K00371) or the periplasmic Nap system (K02567, K02568). Either system completes the nitrate transformation step.

name: Nitrite reduction to Nitric Oxide
notes: Nitrite reduction to nitric oxide (NO) is carried out by either NirS (K00368) or NirK (K15864). Presence of either gene indicates capacity for nitrate/nitrite reduction in denitrification.

name: Nitric Oxide reduction to Nitrous Oxide
notes: The conversion of nitric oxide (NO) to nitrous oxide (N₂O) is catalyzed by nitric oxide reductase, encoded by norB (K04561) in bacteria or CYP55 (K15877) in fungi. Presence of either gene indicates the capacity to perform this denitrification step

name: Nitrous Oxide reduction to Dinitrogen gas
notes: The reduction of nitrous oxide (N₂O) to dinitrogen gas (N₂) is catalyzed by nitrous oxide reductase (nosZ, K00376). Presence of this gene indicates the potential for the final step of denitrification, converting greenhouse gas N₂O into inert atmospheric N₂.

name: Sulfate Reduction
notes: A genome that encodes adenylysulfate reductase and dissimilatory sulfite reductase

name: Tetrathionate Reduction
notes: Tetrathionate reductase complex (ttrABC): TtrA catalytic subunit (K08359), TtrB electron transfer subunit (K08358), TtrC membrane anchor (K08357). At least 2 of 3 subunits required to allow for incomplete genome recovery. Tetrathionate is generated in the inflamed gut from host-derived thiosulfate oxidation and is exploited as an electron acceptor by Salmonella enterica and other Enterobacteriaceae during inflammation, conferring a growth advantage. Rule mirrors Thiosulfate Reduction group — both are non-sulfate sulfur respiration pathways enriched during gut dysbiosis.

name: Fumarate respiration
notes: Presence of both succinate dehydrogenase (K00239–K00242) and fumarate reductase (K00244–K00247) indicates capacity for fumarate respiration, in which fumarate and succinate are interconverted via membrane-bound electron transport complexes. This allows microbes to use fumarate as an electron acceptor or to oxidize succinate as part of a truncated TCA/respiratory chain, a process that can act as a succinate-consuming pathway in the gut and influence luminal succinate levels and host responses

name: TMAO reduction
notes: TMAO reductase systems: TorA (K03532) or TorZ/BisZ (K07811) catalytic subunit paired with TorC (K03533) or TorY/BisC (K07821) cytochrome c subunit. Either complete reductase system (TorAC or TorZY) indicates anaerobic TMAO respiration capacity. TMAO is an abundant dietary-derived compound in fish and meat; gut Enterobacteriaceae reduce it to TMA, which is subsequently oxidized by the host liver to TMAO — connecting microbial metabolism to host cardiovascular risk.

name: Oxidative Stress Response
notes: Presence of oxidative stress response genes indicates microbial potential to detoxify reactive oxygen species through catalase-peroxidase, superoxide dismutase, glutathione biosynthesis, or NADH peroxidase. In the gut, oxidative stress tolerance is particularly relevant during host inflammatory responses where epithelial ROS production increases dramatically, creating oxidizing conditions that challenge strict anaerobes and favor facultative anaerobes and potential pathogens. Capacity for ROS detoxification supports microbial survival and persistence under inflammatory conditions associated with IBD and dysbiosis.

name: Sugar Compatible Solutes [Trehalose]
notes: Presence of trehalose biosynthesis or metabolism genes indicates microbial potential to produce or cycle trehalose, an osmoprotectant that helps maintain cellular water balance under osmotic stress. In the gut, osmotic fluctuations occur in response to dietary changes, host secretions, and luminal water absorption — trehalose producers may be better buffered against these shifts and during host immune responses.

name: Sugar Compatible Solutes [Mannitol]
notes: Presence of mannitol biosynthesis genes indicates microbial potential to produce mannitol, a sugar alcohol osmoprotectant supporting cellular protection under osmotic stress. In the gut, mannitol also serves as a fermentable substrate for other microbes, contributing to cross-feeding and SCFA production in the colon.

name: Sugar Compatible Solutes [Mannosylglycerate]
notes: Presence of mannosylglycerate biosynthesis genes indicates microbial potential to produce mannosylglycerate, a compatible solute that supports osmotic and stress tolerance.

name: Non-Sugar Compatible Solutes
notes: Presence of non-sugar compatible solute biosynthesis genes indicates microbial potential to produce osmoprotectants such as proline or glycerol, supporting cellular water balance under osmotic stress. Relevant to gut microbes navigating the shifting osmotic conditions of the intestinal lumen, including those imposed by host fluid absorption and high-solute diet.

name: Heat Shock Response
notes: Heat shock chaperones and proteases. DnaK (K04043) and DnaJ (K04079) form the core chaperone system; GroEL/GroES (K04080, K04081) provide folding assistance; GrpE (K03686) is the nucleotide exchange factor; ClpB (K03695) disaggregates protein aggregates; ClpXP (K03687) and HslUV are ATP-dependent proteases for misfolded proteins. In the gut, heat shock response is relevant during febrile illness, host inflammatory responses, and thermal shifts encountered during transit from the external environment to the intestinal lumen.

name: Cold Shock Response
notes: Cold shock response via cold shock proteins (CspA family; K10257) acting as RNA chaperones, RecA (K03704) for SOS response, trigger factor (K02834) as ribosome-associated chaperone, and CsdA/DeaD (K05592) cold-inducible DEAD-box RNA helicase. In the gut context, cold shock proteins aid recovery after environmental stress during host ingestion of cold food or drink, and stabilize mRNA secondary structures that form at lower temperatures encountered outside the host.

name: Methyl-Related Compatible Solutes Biosynthesis
notes: Presence of methyl-related compatible solute biosynthesis genes indicates microbial potential to produce glycine betaine or related osmoprotectants that help maintain cellular water balance under osmotic stress. In the gut, glycine betaine also serves as a substrate for TMA production (via betaine reductase pathways) and as a methyl donor, connecting osmoprotection to host metabolite production and one-carbon metabolism.

name: Exopolysaccharide [EPS]
notes: Presence of any listed exopolysaccharide or capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis gene (for example colanic‑acid, PNAG/poly‑GlcNAc, alginate, Psl, or Pss‑like systems) indicates microbial potential for EPS production in human gut and rumen environments, supporting colonization, persistence, and surface or matrix‑associated growth.

name: Biofilms
notes: Biofilm matrix genes subset drawn from the EPS gene pool: colanic acid (K19290/K19291/K19293–K19296), PNAG/poly-GlcNAc biosynthesis (K11936/K11937/K21001), and PGA export/regulation (K20997/K25205/K21461). Presence of any listed gene indicates matrix-associated growth potential. FLAG: rule is intentionally broad pending KA finalization — flagged for review before final release.

name: Quorum Sensing
notes: Quorum sensing via three systems: (1) AHL/LuxI-LuxR: LuxI-type AHL synthases lasI (K13060) or rhlI/cepI/tofI homologs (K13061) paired with LuxR-type receptors lasR (K18304) or rhlR homologs (K18099) — both synthase and receptor required; (2) AI-2/LuxS system: LuxS S-ribosylhomocysteine lyase (K07173) — widely conserved but interpret alone cautiously as it has metabolic roles beyond QS; (3) AI-2 import via Lsr ABC transporter: LsrB substrate-binding (K10555), LsrC permease (K10556), LsrD permease (K10557), LsrA ATPase (K10558) — at least 2 subunits required — indicates active AI-2 uptake and response capacity.

name: Motility
notes: Flagellar motor (MotA K02410 or MotB K02411; at least one required) plus at least 3 structural/assembly genes from the flagellar complex. Required for surface approach and early biofilm attachment. Also relevant for chemotaxis toward carbon/electron donor sources in engineered systems.

name: Bile acid deconjugation
notes: Presence of choloylglycine hydrolase (K01442), the canonical bile salt hydrolase (BSH), indicates capacity to deconjugate glycine- and taurine-conjugated bile acids to free bile acids and amino acids

name: Secondary bile acid synthesis
notes: Co-occurrence of bile acid–CoA ligase (baiB, K15868), 3α-hydroxy bile acid–CoA 3-dehydrogenase (baiA, K15869), and bile-acid 7α-dehydratase (baiE, K15872) marks a bai-type 7α-dehydroxylation pathway. Genomes satisfying this rule are high-confidence secondary bile acid producers capable of converting primary bile acids (e.g., cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid) into secondary bile acids (e.g., deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid) in the human gut

name: Bile acid redox
notes: Presence of at least one bile acid–active hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase indicates capacity to oxidize and epimerize bile acids at the 3 or 7 positions via oxo intermediates. These enzymes are essential for forming iso‑ and urso‑bile acids and for completing epi‑bile acid pathways in the human gut

name: Menaquinone (K2)
notes: Co-occurrence of menF (K02552), menD (K02551), menC (K02549), menB (K01661), menE (K01911), and menA (K02548) represents the full classical menaquinone biosynthesis pathway from chorismate to polyprenylated menaquinone

name: Folate
notes: Co-occurrence of dihydropteroate synthase (K00796) and dihydrofolate reductase (K00287) marks the minimal two-step folate synthesis/recycling module from p-aminobenzoate to tetrahydrofolate. Folate-prototrophic gut microbes (Lactobacillus reuteri, Bifidobacterium spp.) supply folate to the host and folate-auxotrophic microbiome members, supporting one-carbon metabolism and nucleotide synthesis.

name: Thiamine
notes: Co-occurrence of thiamine-phosphate pyrophosphorylase (K03147/ThiE) and hydroxyethylthiazole kinase (K00788/ThiM) marks the minimal thiamine biosynthesis completion module. Thiamine-producing gut microbes contribute to host B1 supply and support TPP-dependent metabolic pathways in the microbiome. Full de novo synthesis requires additional ThiC/ThiG upstream enzymes not captured here; this rule flags thiamine phosphate assembly capacity.

name: Biotin (B7)
notes: Biotin synthase (K01012/BioB) catalyzes the final step of biotin biosynthesis, inserting a sulfur atom into dethiobiotin to form biotin (vitamin B7). Presence alone indicates biotin biosynthesis completion capacity. Biotin-prototrophic gut microbes (Fusobacterium nucleatum, some Bacteroides) contribute to colonic biotin supply; biotin is essential for carboxylase enzymes including pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

name: Niacin (B3)
notes: Co-occurrence of aspartate oxidase (K03517/NadB), quinolinate synthase (K00278/NadA), and nicotinate-nucleotide pyrophosphorylase (K00767/NadC) marks the de novo NAD biosynthesis route from aspartate through quinolinate. Niacin/B3-prototrophic gut microbes produce nicotinamide and support luminal NAD+ precursor availability, relevant for host intestinal epithelial function and microbiome-host signaling via extracellular NAD+ metabolites.

name: Cobalamin (B12)
notes: Presence of all core corrinoid loop assembly genes in KEGG module M00122 (cobyrinate a,c-diamide → cobalamin), with allowed alternatives at specific steps, indicates capacity for de novo completion of cobalamin (vitamin B12) biosynthesis. This marks high-confidence B12 producers in gut and rumen microbiomes, which can support cobalamin-dependent pathways in both microbes and the host.

name: Pantothenate (B5)
notes: Presence of all core pantothenate biosynthesis genes from either the valine/aspartate route (M00119) or the 2‑oxoisovalerate/spermine route (M00913) indicates de novo vitamin B5 production capacity.

name: Pyridoxine (B6)
notes: Presence of all core genes in KEGG module M00124 (erythrose-4P → pyridoxal 5'-phosphate) indicates capacity for de novo vitamin B6 biosynthesis as PLP. In gut and rumen microbiomes, such B6 prototrophy is less prevalent than other B-vitamin pathways but supports amino acid metabolism and can provide B6 to auxotrophic microbes and the host

name: Riboflavin (B2)
notes: Presence of all core genes in KEGG module M00125 (riboflavin biosynthesis, GTP → riboflavin/FM N/FAD) with allowed enzyme alternatives indicates capacity for de novo vitamin B2 biosynthesis. In gut and rumen microbiomes, such riboflavin prototrophy is an important microbial trait that supplies B2 for FMN/FAD cofactor production and can contribute to host vitamin status

name: TMA production
notes: TMA production via three routes: (1) choline TMA-lyase complex cutC/cutD (K20038/K20037) — primary choline-to-TMA route; (2) carnitine oxygenase cntA (K22443) — L-carnitine cleavage; (3) glycine reductase grdH (K21579) — glycine betaine reduction. TMA is the gut microbial precursor of host-produced TMAO, a circulating metabolite associated with cardiovascular disease risk. All three routes are diet-substrate-dependent.

name: TMA demethylation
notes: TMA demethylation via pyrrolysine-containing methyltransferases: MttB-type trimethylamine methyltransferase (K14083), MtgB glycine betaine methyltransferase (K25600), or EC:2.1.1.389 (dimethylamine/trimethylamine corrinoid methyltransferase). Removes a methyl group from TMA, reducing circulating TMA and potentially TMAO levels. Found in Methanomassiliicoccales archaea and some anaerobic bacteria. NOTE: EC:2.1.1.389 is not yet a KEGG K-number — confirm DRAM2 can accept EC:identifiers in rule engine.

name: Beta-Lactam Resistance
notes: Beta-lactamase and penicillin-binding protein resistance genes conferring resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems). Major antibiotic resistance gene class in environmental microbiomes.

name: Macrolide Resistance
notes: Macrolide resistance via efflux pumps, ribosomal methylases (erm genes), or macrolide esterases.

name: Tetracycline Resistance
notes: Tetracycline resistance via efflux pumps (tet efflux genes) or ribosomal protection proteins.

name: Sulfonamide Resistance
notes: Sulfonamide resistance via dihydropteroate synthase variants (sul1, sul2, sul3) insensitive to sulfonamide inhibition. Sulfonamide resistance genes are among the most prevalent antibiotic resistance determinants in human gut microbiomes, particularly in individuals with prior antibiotic exposure, and are frequently found on mobile genetic elements that co-carry other resistance genes.

name: Aminoglycoside Resistance
notes: Presence of aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme genes, including N-acetyltransferases (AAC(3), AAC(6′)), O-nucleotidyltransferases (aadA, ANT(3ʺ); K00984), and O-phosphotransferases (APH(3′), APH(3ʺ)), indicates resistance to aminoglycoside antibiotics via drug inactivation. Aminoglycoside resistance genes of these families are common in human and animal gut microbiomes and in the rumen, where they contribute substantially to the overall resistome

name: Glycopeptide Resistance
notes: Presence of all core genes in KEGG module M00651, encoding the D-Ala–D-Lac type vancomycin resistance cluster, indicates capacity to replace the D-Ala–D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors with D-Ala–D-Lac and thereby reduce vancomycin binding. This mechanism is characteristic of vancomycin-resistant enterococci and other glycopeptide-resistant Gram-positive bacteria and can occur in gut and rumen microbiomes as part of the glycopeptide resistome

name: Prodrug activation
notes: Prodrug activation: azoreductase (K01118) reduces azo-bond prodrugs (sulfasalazine, balsalazide) to release active 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) in the colon. Primary enzymatic mechanism by which IBD prodrugs are activated by gut microbiota. Presence indicates capacity to convert prodrugs to their active forms, with implications for inter-individual variation in drug response.

name: Chemotherapy inactivation
notes: Chemotherapy inactivation: co-occurrence of cytosine deaminase (K17722) and uracil phosphoribosyltransferase (K17723) encodes the 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) inactivation pathway. Gut microbes expressing these enzymes can degrade 5-FU to inactive catabolites, potentially reducing drug efficacy. Relevant to colorectal cancer chemotherapy outcomes where microbiome composition affects 5-FU bioavailability.

name: Nitro drug reduction
notes: Nitro drug reduction: nitroreductase type I (K10678) or type II (K10679) reduces nitro groups in prodrugs such as metronidazole, nitrofurantoin, and tinidazole. Reductive activation converts these prodrugs to toxic intermediates that damage DNA. Paradoxically, acquired resistance in Helicobacter pylori and Bacteroides involves loss or mutation of these reductases — flagging presence indicates susceptibility to nitro-drug activation.

name: Neurological drugs
notes: Levodopa decarboxylase / aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (K22330/TyrDC) decarboxylates L-DOPA to dopamine in the gut lumen. Gut microbial DOPA decarboxylation reduces levodopa bioavailability and is a key mechanism underlying inter-individual variation in Parkinson's disease treatment efficacy. Inhibiting gut microbial K22330 activity is an active therapeutic target.

name: Isoflavonoid metabolism
notes: Captures anoxic isoflavonoid conversion pathway (daidzein/genistein → equol). Equol production is entirely microbiome-dependent and clinically relevant for estrogen-like activity

name: Flavonoid degradation
notes: Covers anoxic flavone/flavonol degradation to phloroglucinol (K26176-K26178, K22906), quercetin degradation oxic (K07155, K06911), and naringenin degradation oxic (K26179-K26185)

name: Tannin & phenolic acid metabolism
notes: Covers tannin hydrolysis (K10759/tannase), gallate conversion to pyrogallol anoxic (K22958-K22960) and oxic (K04099), ferulic acid conversion to vanillin (K12508, K18383), and caffeate respiration anoxic (K22430-K22432)

name: Urease
notes: Urea hydrolysis requires the full urease enzyme complex composed of subunits ureC (K01428), ureB (K01429), and ureA (K01430). All three subunits are required for activity. In the gut, urease-positive organisms (Helicobacter pylori, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis) hydrolyze urea to ammonia and CO₂, raising local pH and supporting colonization of acidic niches. In the rumen, urease activity by diverse Firmicutes and Proteobacteria is central to urea nitrogen recycling and represents a major route by which dietary or salivary urea re-enters the microbial nitrogen pool

name: Iron acquisition
notes: Siderophore receptors (K19611/fepA, K16090/fiu, K16091/fecA), heme acquisition (K12545/hasA, K16152/hasR), siderophore/yersiniabactin receptors (K15721/fyuA), and iron complex TonB-dependent receptors (K16088, K16089, K16087, K02014). Broad outer-membrane iron uptake capacity.

name: Hemolysins
notes: Pore-forming hemolysins: HlyA (K11005), HlyII (K11032), leukocidin/Hlg family (K11038), and HlyC-family protein (K06189). Note: K06189 and K11005/K11032/K11038 are also present in Toxins row — expected overlap between hemolysin and toxin categories.

name: Pilus and Fimbrial Adhesion
notes: Surface attachment to gut epithelium via fimbrial and pilus systems.

name: Epithelial invasion
notes: Active invasion of gut epithelial cells via multiple mechanisms.

name: Type III Secretion System
notes: Type III secretion system capacity via structural components or secreted effectors

name: Type VI Secretion System
notes: Type VI secretion system capacity via Hcp tube proteins or VgrG spike proteins.

name: IgA Protease
notes: IgA1 protease (K01347) cleaves human immunoglobulin IgA1 at the hinge region, inactivating mucosal antibody defense. Produced by Neisseria, Haemophilus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae as a major immune evasion strategy in mucosal pathogens. In the gut, IgA protease activity can disrupt the secretory IgA coat that normally excludes commensal and pathogenic bacteria from the epithelium.

name: Toxins
notes: Covers genotoxins (CDT K11014, colibactin K26579), pore-forming/hemolysins (K06189, K11005, K11032, K11038), ER stress (subtilase K19297/K19298), vacuolating (VacA K11028), heat-labile enterotoxin complex (K10928+K10929), heat-stable enterotoxin (K16883/K16884), Shiga toxin (K11006/K11007)
